claim: SARM1 displays NADase activity that depletes the key cellular metabolite, NAD+, in response to nerve injury.
source: SARM1, an executor of axonal degeneration, displays NADase activity that depletes the key cellular metabolite, NAD+, in response to nerve injury.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of SARM1, supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: SARM1 homo-octamer avoids premature activation by assuming a packed conformation with ordered inner and peripheral rings.
source: These indicate that SARM1 homo-octamer avoids premature activation by assuming a packed conformation, with ordered inner and peripheral rings, that prevents dimerization and activation of the catalytic domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM structural data presented in the manuscript at 2.9 and 2.7 Å resolutions.

claim: The packed conformation of SARM1 prevents dimerization and activation of the catalytic domains.
source: These indicate that SARM1 homo-octamer avoids premature activation by assuming a packed conformation, with ordered inner and peripheral rings, that prevents dimerization and activation of the catalytic domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing TIR domains separated in the compact conformation.

claim: The inactive conformation of SARM1 is stabilized by binding of NAD+ in an allosteric location away from the catalytic sites.
source: This inactive conformation is stabilized by binding of SARM1's own substrate NAD+ in an allosteric location, away from the catalytic sites.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM density maps showing NAD+ bound at the ARM domain 'horns' region.

claim: Mutagenesis of the allosteric site led to constitutively active SARM1.
source: This model was validated by mutagenesis of the allosteric site, which led to constitutively active SARM1.
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assays showing that mutations at the allosteric site induce cell death.

claim: The reduction of cellular NAD+ concentration contributes to the disassembly of SARM1's peripheral ring.
source: We propose that the reduction of cellular NAD+ concentration contributes to the disassembly of SARM1's peripheral ring, which allows formation of active NADase domain dimers, thereby further depleting NAD+ to cause an energetic catastrophe and cell death.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SARM1 was first discovered as a negative regulator of TRIF in TLR signaling.
source: SARM1 (sterile α and HEAT/armadillo motif–containing protein; Mink et al., 2001) was first discovered as a negative regulator of TRIF (TIR domain–containing adaptor inducing interferon-β) in TLR (Toll-like receptor) signaling (Carty et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carty et al., 2006.

claim: SARM1 promotes neuronal death by oxygen and glucose deprivation.
source: SARM1 was later shown to promote neuronal death by oxygen and glucose deprivation (Kim et al., 2007) and viral infections (Hou et al., 2013; Mukherjee et al., 2013; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2020; Uccellini et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2007.

claim: SARM1 has a protective role against bacterial and fungal infections in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: while also having a protective role against bacterial and fungal infections in Caenorhabditis elegans (Couillault et al., 2004; Liberati et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Couillault et al., 2004 and Liberati et al., 2004.

claim: SARM1 is a key part of a highly conserved axonal death pathway that is activated by nerve injury.
source: Subsequently, studies have demonstrated that SARM1 is also a key part of a highly conserved axonal death pathway that is activated by nerve injury (Gerdts et al., 2013; Osterloh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gerdts et al., 2013 and Osterloh et al., 2012.

claim: SARM1 deficiency confers protection against axonal degeneration in several models of neurodegenerative conditions.
source: Notably, SARM1 deficiency confers protection against axonal degeneration in several models of neurodegenerative conditions (Kim et al., 2007; Ko et al., 2020; Ozaki et al., 2020; Uccellini et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: SARM1 is a compelling drug target to protect axons in a variety of axonopathies.
source: making SARM1 a compelling drug target to protect axons in a variety of axonopathies (Krauss et al., 2020; Loring et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Krauss et al., 2020 and Loring et al., 2020.

claim: The domain composition of SARM1 includes an N-terminal peptide, an ARM-repeats region, two SAM, and one TIR domain.
source: The domain composition of SARM1 includes an N-terminal peptide, an ARM-repeats region, two SAM, and one TIR domain (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The N-terminal peptide of SARM1 mediates mitochondria targeting.
source: which mediate mitochondria targeting (Panneerselvam et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Panneerselvam et al., 2012.

claim: The ARM-repeats region of SARM1 mediates auto-inhibition.
source: auto-inhibition (Chuang and Bargmann, 2005; Summers et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chuang and Bargmann, 2005 and Summers et al., 2016.

claim: The SAM domains of SARM1 mediate oligomerization.
source: oligomerization (Gerdts et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gerdts et al., 2013.

claim: The TIR domain of SARM1 mediates NADase activity.
source: and NADase activity (Gerdts et al., 2015), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gerdts et al., 2015.

claim: Amino acid substitutions E642A or E596K at the TIR domain's active site abolish the NADase activity in vitro.
source: Amino acid substitutions (E642A or E596K) at the TIR domain's active site abolish the NADase activity in vitro and inactivates SARM1 pro-degenerative activity (Essuman et al., 2017; Geisler et al., 2019; Horsefield et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Essuman et al., 2017, Geisler et al., 2019, and Horsefield et al., 2019.

claim: The enzymatic activity of SARM1 requires a high local concentration of the TIR domains.
source: The enzymatic activity requires a high local concentration of the TIR domains, as demonstrated by forced dimerization of TIR, which resulted in NAD+ hydrolysis and neuronal cell death (Gerdts et al., 2015; Gerdts et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gerdts et al., 2015 and Gerdts et al., 2016.

claim: Deletion of the ARM domain in SARM1 renders the 'delARM' construct constitutively active and leads to rapid cell death.
source: Also, the deletion of the ARM domain in SARM1, which interacts directly with TIR (Summers et al., 2016), renders the 'delARM' construct constitutively active and leads to rapid cell death (Gerdts et al., 2013; Sporny et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gerdts et al., 2013 and Sporny et al., 2019.

claim: Both hSARM1 and the isolated tandem SAM1–2 domains form octamers in solution.
source: where we showed that both hSARM1 (human SARM1) and the isolated tandem SAM1–2 domains form octamers in solution.
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous study (Sporny et al., 2019).

claim: Negative stain electron microscopy analysis of hSARM1 revealed an octameric ring arrangement.
source: In this study, we used negative stain electron microscopy analysis of hSARM1 and determined the crystal structure (as did others [Horsefield et al., 2019]) of the SAM1–2 domains – both of which revealed an octameric ring arrangement.
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous study (Sporny et al., 2019) and cited work by Horsefield et al., 2019.

claim: SARM1 gains NADase activity upon stress conditions through various insults including axotomy, oxidation, metabolic conditions, or toxins.
source: These findings imply that hSARM1 is kept auto-inhibited by the ARM domain in homeostasis and gains NADase activity upon stress conditions through the following: the infliction of injury (axotomy, Osterloh et al., 2012), oxidation (mitochondria depolarization, Murata et al., 2013; oxidizing agents, Summers et al., 2014), metabolic conditions (depletion of NAD+, Gilley et al., 2015), or toxins (chemotherapy drugs, Geisler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is potentially involved in promoting the NADase activity of SARM1.
source: In this regard, little is known about the direct molecular triggers of SARM1 in cells, besides the potential involvement of nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) (Bratkowski et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2018a; Zhao et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bratkowski et al., 2020, Liu et al., 2018a, and Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: Ser-548 phosphorylation by c-Jun N-terminal kinase is potentially involved in promoting the NADase activity of SARM1.
source: and Ser-548 phosphorylation by c-Jun N-terminal kinase (Murata et al., 2018) in promoting the NADase activity of SARM1.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Murata et al., 2018.

claim: SARM1 is kept inactive through a 'substrate inhibition' mechanism where high concentration of NAD+ stabilizes the tightly packed, inhibited conformation of the protein.
source: Here, we present structural data and complementary biochemical assays to show that SARM1 is kept inactive through a 'substrate inhibition' mechanism, where the high concentration of NAD+ stabilizes the tightly packed, inhibited conformation of the protein.
evidence: This is supported by structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SARM1 activation is triggered by a decrease in the concentration of cellular metabolite NAD+.
source: In this way, SARM1 activation is triggered by a decrease in the concentration of a cellular metabolite NAD+, rather than depending on the introduction of an activating factor.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The hSARM1E642Q construct lacks the N-terminal mitochondrial localization signal and has a point mutation in the NADase catalytic site.
source: For cryo-EM imaging, we generated a near-intact hSARM1 construct that lacks the N-terminal mitochondrial localization signal (26ERL…GPT724) and has a point mutation in the NADase catalytic site (E642Q).
evidence: This is a description of the construct used in the study.

claim: 2D classification and 3D reconstruction of purified hSARM1E642Q revealed an octamer ring assembly with clearly visible inner ring attributed to the tandem SAM domains.
source: 2D classification (Figure 1C) and 3D reconstruction (Figure 1D, Table 1) revealed an octamer ring assembly with clearly visible inner ring, which is attributed to the tandem SAM domains.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Only a minor fraction (~20%) of the hSARM1E642Q particles shows the presence of a (partial) peripheral ring composed by the ARM and TIR domains.
source: Only a minor fraction of the particles (~20%) shows the presence of a (partial) peripheral ring composed by the ARM and TIR domains.
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM analysis of the purified protein.

claim: The ARM and TIR domains are largely missing from the cryo-EM reconstruction of hSARM1E642Q, implying a disordered peripheral ring in ~80% of the particles.
source: Cryo-EM analysis of the isolated SAM1–2 domains (Figure 1D) and docking of the crystal structure of the SAM1–2 octamer (PDB code 6QWV) into the 3D maps demonstrate that indeed the ARM and TIR domains are largely missing from this reconstruction, implying a disordered peripheral ring in ~80% of the particles.
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM analysis and comparison with the SAM1-2 structure.

claim: Exploring different buffers, pH and salt conditions, addition of various detergents, as well as variations in cryo-EM grid preparation did not affect the visibility of the octamer peripheral ring considerably.
source: Exploring different buffers, pH and salt conditions, addition of various detergents, as well as variations in cryo-EM grid preparation (e.g. ice thickness) did not affect the visibility of the octamer peripheral ring considerably.
evidence: This describes experimental attempts to improve the structural visualization.

claim: The GraFix-ed hSARM1E642Q octamer is 203 Å in diameter and 80 Å thick.
source: The hSARM1E642Q octamer is 203 Å in diameter and 80 Å thick (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a measurement from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The SAM1–2 domains' inner ring is the best resolved part of the GraFix-ed hSARM1E642Q map.
source: The SAM1–2 domains' inner ring is the best resolved part of the map to which the high-resolution crystal structure (PDB code 6QWV) was fitted with minute adjustments.
evidence: This is based on the quality of the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The TIR domains are the least defined part of the GraFix-ed hSARM1E642Q density map.
source: The TIR domains are the least defined part of the density map.
evidence: This is based on the quality of the cryo-EM density map.

claim: Some parts of the TIR domain reach a local resolution of 6.5 Å.
source: Some parts of the TIR domain reach a local resolution of 6.5 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) and therefore not revealing side chain positions.
evidence: This is based on local resolution analysis of the cryo-EM map.

claim: High-resolution crystal structures of isolated hSARM1 TIR allowed their docking into the well-resolved secondary structure elements in the map with very high confidence.
source: However, the availability of high-resolution crystal structures of isolated hSARM1 TIR (PDB codes 6O0R, 6O0U; Horsefield et al., 2019) allowed their docking into the well-resolved secondary structure elements in the map with very high confidence.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach using existing crystal structures.

claim: The ARM domains show intermediate map quality, with well-resolved secondary structures and bulky side chains.
source: The ARM domains show intermediate map quality, with well-resolved secondary structures and bulky side chains.
evidence: This is based on the quality of the cryo-EM density map.

claim: A de-novo atomic model for the entire ARM domain was built.
source: This allowed the building of a de-novo atomic model for the entire ARM, as no high-resolution structure or homology models of SARM1's ARM are available.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach for the ARM domain.

claim: The entire atomic model of GraFix-ed hSARM1E642Q is comprised of residues 56–700.
source: The entire atomic model is comprised of residues 56–700 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), with an internal break at the linker that connects SAM2 to the TIR domain.
evidence: This describes the extent of the atomic model built.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the ARM domain reveals a closed crescent-shaped region, composed of seven three-helix ARM repeats spanning residues 60–400.
source: The cryo-EM structure of the ARM domain reveals a closed crescent-shaped region, composed of seven three-helix ARM repeats spanning residues 60–400 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure of the ARM domain.

claim: The ARM topology is split into two interacting parts, designated ARM1 (res. 60–303 with five ARM repeats) and ARM2 (res. 322–400 with two ARM repeats).
source: The ARM topology is split into two interacting parts, designated ARM1 (res. 60–303 with five ARM repeats) and ARM2 (res. 322–400 with two ARM repeats) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure of the ARM domain.

claim: The main ARM1–ARM2 interaction interface is hydrophobic and involves helices α14 and α16 of ARM1 and helices α1, α2, and α3 of ARM2.
source: The main ARM1–ARM2 interaction interface is hydrophobic and involves helices α14 and α16 of ARM1 and helices α1, α2, and α3 of ARM2.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: ARM1 and ARM2 interact at the crescent 'horns' through the ARM1α2–α3 loop with the loop that connects ARM1 with ARM2 (res. 305–320).
source: ARM1 and ARM2 are also interacting at the crescent 'horns' through the ARM1α2–α3 loop with the loop that connects ARM1 with ARM2 (res. 305–320).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: In the hSARM1 compact octamer, each ARM is directly connected via a linker (res. 400–404) to a SAM1 domain.
source: In the hSARM1 compact octamer, each ARM is directly connected via a linker (res. 400–404) to a SAM1 domain.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Each ARM is engaged in several non-covalent interactions with the same-chain SAM and with the clockwise neighboring SAM.
source: Also, each ARM is engaged in several non-covalent interactions with the same-chain SAM and with the clockwise neighboring SAM, when assuming a top view of the structure (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Direct interactions between neighboring ARM domains are limited, engaging a short segment of ARM1 α9 with the α4–α5 loop of ARM2 of the neighboring chain.
source: Although neighboring ARM domains are closely packed, direct interactions between them seem to be limited, engaging a short segment of ARM1 α9 with the α4–α5 loop of ARM2 of the neighboring chain.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Additional ARM–ARM interactions are indirect, mediated by the TIR domains.
source: Additional ARM–ARM interactions are indirect, mediated by the TIR domains.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Each TIR binds the ARM ring via two sites, designated the 'primary' and 'secondary' TIR docking sites.
source: Each TIR binds the ARM ring via two sites, designated the 'primary' and 'secondary' TIR docking sites (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The 'primary' TIR docking site is larger and engages the TIR helix αA and the EE loop with the ARM1 α10, α10–α11 loop, and α13.
source: The 'primary' is larger and engages the TIR helix αA and the EE loop with the ARM1 α10, α10–α11 loop, and α13.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The 'secondary' TIR docking site is smaller and involves the TIR BB loop and helix α7 of the counter-clockwise ARM1 domain.
source: The 'secondary' TIR docking site is smaller and involves the TIR BB loop and helix α7 of the counter-clockwise ARM1 domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The GraFix-ed cryo-EM structure revealed a domain organization where the catalytic TIR subunits are separated from each other by docking onto the ARM peripheral ring.
source: The GraFix-ed cryo-EM structure revealed a domain organization where the catalytic TIR subunits are separated from each other by docking onto the ARM peripheral ring.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The assembly of TIR domains in the compact conformation is dependent on the coupling of each TIR with two neighboring ARM domains.
source: This assembly is dependent on the coupling of each TIR with two neighboring ARM domains (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The NADase activity of SARM1 requires close proximity of several TIR domains.
source: Since the NADase activity requires close proximity of several TIR domains (Bratkowski et al., 2020; Gerdts et al., 2015; Gerdts et al., 2016), and possibly homo-dimerization (Horsefield et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cryo-EM structure represents an inhibited conformation of SARM1, in which the TIR domains cannot form compact dimers and catabolize NAD+.
source: we considered that the cryo-EM structure represents an inhibited conformation of SARM1, in which the TIR domains cannot form compact dimers and catabolize NAD+.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and known requirements for NADase activity.

claim: Mutations RR216-7EE and FP255-6RR at the ARM's primary TIR docking site were designed to weaken TIR docking.
source: To this end we designed amino acid substitutions at the ARM's primary TIR docking site without compromising the protein's structural integrity – particularly that of the TIR domain (Figure 3A). Two pairs of mutations, RR216-7EE of ARM1 helix α10 and FP255-6RR of ARM1 helix α13 (Figure 3C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), were introduced, as well as the double mutant RR216-7EE/FP255-6RR.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for testing the role of the primary TIR docking site.

claim: The FP255-6RR and double mutant RR216-7EE/FP255-6RR showed a rapid decrease in cellular NAD+ levels and 50% cell death within 24 hr after transfection.
source: The results (Figure 3C) show a rapid decrease in cellular NAD+ levels and 50% cell death within 24 hr after transfection of the FP255-6RR and double mutant.
evidence: This is based on cell viability assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The toxicity level of FP255-6RR and double mutant is similar to that of the 'delARM' construct.
source: This toxicity level is similar to that of a hSARM1 construct missing the entire ARM domain 'delARM' (res. 409–724) (Figure 3C), proven to be toxic in neurons and HEK293 cells (Gerdts et al., 2013; Sporny et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on comparison of cell viability assays.

claim: The RR216-7EE mutation has a weaker effect, probably due to the position of these amino acid residues at the margin of the TIR-ARM interface.
source: The RR216-7EE mutation has a weaker effect, probably due to the position of these amino acid residues at the margin of the TIR-ARM interface.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on structural analysis.

claim: hSARM1 inhibition requires ARM-TIR interaction through the 'primary TIR docking site'.
source: In conclusion, we found that hSARM1 inhibition requires ARM-TIR interaction through the 'primary TIR docking site'.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The surface-exposed residues at the ARM-TIR interface reveal a high level of conservation.
source: The surface-exposed residues reveal a high level of conservation on both the ARM and TIR domain–binding interface.
evidence: This is based on conservation analysis using the Consurf server.

claim: The high conservation at the ARM-TIR interface indicates the biological importance of the interface and a possible conservation of its function in auto-inhibition among species.
source: This indicates the biological importance of the interface and a possible conservation of its function in auto-inhibition among species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation analysis.

claim: The purified hSARM1 that was not subjected to GraFix and predominantly presents just the inner SAM ring in cryo-EM is active in vitro.
source: As it became clear that the compact two-ring structure is inhibited for NADase activity, we considered whether the purified hSARM1, that was not subjected to GraFix and predominantly presents just the inner SAM ring in cryo-EM 2D averaging and 3D reconstruction (Figure 1C and D), is active in vitro.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by in vitro NADase activity assays.

claim: Purified hSARM1w.t. has a Km of 28 ± 4 µM for NAD+.
source: Using a resazurin fluorescence assay modified for an in vitro application, we measured the rate of NAD+ consumption by hSARM1w.t. in a series of NAD+ concentrations and determined a Km of 28 ± 4 µM
evidence: This is based on in vitro NADase activity assays.

claim: Purified hSARM1w.t. has a Vmax of 9 ± 0.3 µM/min for NAD+.
source: with Vmax of 9 ± 0.3 µM/min
evidence: This is based on in vitro NADase activity assays.

claim: Purified hSARM1w.t. has a Kcat of 46.49 1/min for NAD+.
source: and Kcat of 46.49 1/min (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on in vitro NADase activity assays.

claim: The kinetic parameters of purified hSARM1w.t. are remarkably similar to a published Km of 24 µM for isolated TIR domain fused to artificial dimerizing and aggregating agents.
source: These kinetic parameters are remarkably similar to a published Km of 24 µM (Essuman et al., 2017) – especially when considering that the quoted study used an isolated TIR domain fused to artificial dimerizing and aggregating agents, while we used the near-intact protein.
evidence: This is a comparison with previously published data.

claim: NMN levels rise after axonal injury.
source: It was previously discovered that NMN levels rise after axonal injury, and that exogenous increase of NMN induces degeneration (Di Stefano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Di Stefano et al., 2015.

claim: A membrane-permeable NMN analogue activates SARM1 in cultured cells, leading to their death.
source: Moreover, a membrane-permeable NMN analogue activates SARM1 in cultured cells, leading to their death (Liu et al., 2018a; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2018a and Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: 1 mM NMN increases hSARM1 activity by ~30%.
source: We therefore measured the effect of NMN supplement on the NADase activity of purified hSARM1 and found a moderate 30% increase in activity with 1 mM NMN, but none at a lower concentration of 200 µM (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on in vitro NADase activity assays with NMN supplement.

claim: 0.2 mM NMN has no visible effect on hSARM1 activity.
source: We therefore measured the effect of NMN supplement on the NADase activity of purified hSARM1 and found a moderate 30% increase in activity with 1 mM NMN, but none at a lower concentration of 200 µM (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on in vitro NADase activity assays with NMN supplement.

claim: The purified hSARM1 is mostly NADase active, even without NMN supplement.
source: This demonstrates that the purified hSARM1 is mostly NADase active, even without NMN supplement, supporting the idea of a predominantly open conformation as seen in cryo-EM (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vitro activity assays and cryo-EM data.

claim: Glycerol reduces hSARM1 NADase activity in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Next, we examined what confines the GraFix-ed hSARM1 into the compact inhibited conformation (Figure 2) and measured the in vitro NADase activity in the presence of glycerol (Figure 3F). We found that glycerol reduces hSARM1 NADase activity in a concentration-dependent manner, reaching 72% inhibition at 15% glycerol.
evidence: This is based on in vitro NADase activity assays with glycerol.

claim: 15% glycerol causes 72% inhibition of hSARM1 NADase activity.
source: We found that glycerol reduces hSARM1 NADase activity in a concentration-dependent manner, reaching 72% inhibition at 15% glycerol.
evidence: This is based on in vitro NADase activity assays with glycerol.

claim: In the GraFix preparation, hSARM1 was extracted from the gradient after it migrated to approximately 18% glycerol concentration.
source: In the GraFix preparation, we extracted hSARM1 from the gradient after it migrated to approximately 18% glycerol concentration.
evidence: This describes the GraFix protocol used.

claim: The compact conformation of hSARM1 is maintained after glycerol is removed, due to glutaraldehyde crosslinking.
source: It seems likely that this conformation is maintained after glycerol is removed, due to glutaraldehyde crosslinking which preserves the compact structure.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of the GraFix protocol.

claim: hSARM1 NADase activity is suppressed in cell culture.
source: Our results show that hSARM1 NADase activity is suppressed in cell culture, but much less so in vitro after being isolated.
evidence: This is based on comparison of cellular and in vitro activity assays.

claim: In the course of purification from the cytosolic fraction, hSARM1 loses a low-affinity cellular factor responsible for inhibiting it in the cellular environment.
source: This prompted us to hypothesize that in the course of purification from the cytosolic fraction, hSARM1 loses a low-affinity cellular factor, responsible for inhibiting it in the cellular environment.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the difference in activity between cellular and in vitro conditions.

claim: The hypothesized inhibitory factor is a small molecule that is depleted under cellular stress conditions.
source: We reasoned that the hypothesized inhibitory factor is a small molecule that is depleted under cellular stress conditions, and thus the inhibition of hSARM1 is released.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known activation conditions of SARM1.

claim: ATP inhibits the NADase activity of hSARM1 in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Indeed, we found that ATP inhibits the NADase activity of hSARM1 in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on in vitro NADase activity assays with ATP.

claim: ATP did not affect hSARM1 conformation as observed by 2D classification.
source: However, it did not affect hSARM1 conformation as observed by 2D classification (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM 2D classification with ATP supplement.

claim: ATP possibly inhibits hSARM1 through the TIR domain's active site.
source: Therefore, it is possible that ATP inhibits hSARM1 through the TIR domain's active site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of conformational change with ATP.

claim: NAD+ levels drop in response to axon injury.
source: It was reported that NAD+ levels drop in response to axon injury (Coleman and Höke, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Coleman and Höke, 2020.

claim: The ablation of the cytosolic NAD+ synthesizing enzymes NMNAT1 and 2 decreases cytoplasmic NAD+ and induces SARM1 activation.
source: Also, the ablation of the cytosolic NAD+ synthesizing enzymes NMNAT1 and 2 decreases cytoplasmic NAD+ and induces SARM1 activation (Gilley et al., 2015; Sasaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gilley et al., 2015 and Sasaki et al., 2016.

claim: Adding 5 mM NAD+ to hSARM1 results in >80% of the particles showing the two-ring, compact conformation in cryo-EM.
source: Cryo-EM images show that adding 5 mM NAD+ to hSARM1 has a dramatic effect: >80% of the particles show the two-ring, compact conformation – in contrast to the <20% found in the absence of NAD+ (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM 2D classification with NAD+ supplement.

claim: Without NAD+ supplement, <20% of hSARM1 particles show the two-ring, compact conformation in cryo-EM.
source: Cryo-EM images show that adding 5 mM NAD+ to hSARM1 has a dramatic effect: >80% of the particles show the two-ring, compact conformation – in contrast to the <20% found in the absence of NAD+ (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM 2D classification without NAD+ supplement.

claim: The highest rate of NAD+ hydrolysis by hSARM1 occurs at 100 µM NAD+.
source: The results showed a bell-shaped curve (Figure 4D) with the highest rate of hydrolysis at 100 µM NAD+ and a steady decrease in rate thereafter (at the higher concentrations).
evidence: This is based on fluorescent assays with eNAD.

claim: hSARM1 shows substrate inhibition at NAD+ concentrations higher than 100 µM.
source: The results showed a bell-shaped curve (Figure 4D) with the highest rate of hydrolysis at 100 µM NAD+ and a steady decrease in rate thereafter (at the higher concentrations).
evidence: This is based on fluorescent assays with eNAD showing a bell-shaped curve.

claim: The rate of hydrolysis of porcine NADase was maintained between 50 µM and 2 mM NAD+.
source: While the rate of hydrolysis of porcine NADase was maintained between 50 µM and 2 mM NAD+, hSARM1 was almost completely inhibited at 2 mM NAD+ (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on HPLC monitoring of NAD+ consumption.

claim: hSARM1 was almost completely inhibited at 2 mM NAD+.
source: While the rate of hydrolysis of porcine NADase was maintained between 50 µM and 2 mM NAD+, hSARM1 was almost completely inhibited at 2 mM NAD+ (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on HPLC monitoring of NAD+ consumption.

claim: hSARM1 supplemented with 5 mM NAD+ was reconstructed and refined to 2.7 Å resolution.
source: hSARM1, supplemented by 5 mM NAD+, was imaged, reconstructed, and refined to 2.7 Å resolution (Figure 5A), resulting in an excellent map (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data collection and processing.

claim: The structure of NAD+ supplemented hSARM1 was largely identical to the GraFix-ed structure.
source: The structure was largely identical to the GraFix-ed structure, further substantiating the validity of the latter (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the two cryo-EM structures.

claim: There is a 5 Å shift in the position of the distal part of the TIR domain between the NAD+ supplemented and GraFix-ed structures.
source: Few structural differences can be observed between the NAD+ supplemented density map and that of the GraFix-ed hSARM1. The first difference is a 5 Å shift in the position of the distal part of the TIR domain
evidence: This is based on comparison of the two cryo-EM structures.

claim: There is a rearrangement of the secondary structure at the region of the 'crescent horns' between the NAD+ supplemented and GraFix-ed structures.
source: and the second is a rearrangement of the secondary structure at the region of the 'crescent horns', where the tips of ARM1 and ARM2 touch (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2A and B).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the two cryo-EM structures.

claim: An extra-density in the NAD+ supplemented map reveals the binding site of one NAD+ molecule at the 'ARM allosteric site'.
source: In the same region, designated hereafter 'ARM allosteric site', an extra-density in the NAD+ supplemented map reveals the binding site of one NAD+ molecule, providing clear atomic details (Figure 5C, right panel).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the NAD+ supplemented cryo-EM map.

claim: Mutations L152A and R157E in the ARM1 α5–α6 loop had a dramatic effect on hSARM1 activity, promoting cell death levels comparable to the 'delARM' construct.
source: Indeed, we found that two separate mutations in the ARM1 α5–α6 loop (L152A and R157E) and one in the opposite ARM1–ARM2 loop (R322E) had a dramatic effect on hSARM1 activity, promoting cell death levels comparable to those induced by the 'delARM' 'constitutively active' construct, which is missing the entire ARM domain (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on cell viability assays.

claim: Mutation R322E in the ARM1–ARM2 loop had a dramatic effect on hSARM1 activity, promoting cell death levels comparable to the 'delARM' construct.
source: Indeed, we found that two separate mutations in the ARM1 α5–α6 loop (L152A and R157E) and one in the opposite ARM1–ARM2 loop (R322E) had a dramatic effect on hSARM1 activity, promoting cell death levels comparable to those induced by the 'delARM' 'constitutively active' construct, which is missing the entire ARM domain (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on cell viability assays.

claim: Mutations D314A and Q320A, located at the ARM1–ARM2 loop but with side chains positioned away from the NAD+ molecule, did not induce hSARM1 activation.
source: Two mutations (D314A and Q320A), which are also located at the ARM1–ARM2 loop but their side chains positioned away from the NAD+ molecule, did not induce hSARM1 activation.
evidence: This is based on cell viability assays.

claim: Control mutations E94R and K363A did not affect hSARM1 activity.
source: As expected, the control mutations E94R and K363A did not affect hSARM1 activity either.
evidence: This is based on cell viability assays.

claim: Mutating W103 to alanine had only a small effect on hSARM1 activity.
source: Surprisingly, mutating the bulky W103, which stacks with the NAD+ nicotinamide ring, into an alanine had only a small effect.
evidence: This is based on cell viability assays.

claim: W103D mutation had strong activating effect on hSARM1.
source: Nevertheless, W103D mutation did have strong activating effect
evidence: This is based on cell viability assays.

claim: NAD+ contacts with the W103 side chain may be dispensable for the NAD+ inhibitory effect, but interference cannot be tolerated.
source: leading to the notion that NAD+ contacts with the W103 side chain may be dispensable for the NAD+ inhibitory effect, but interference (as by the aspartate side chain) cannot be tolerated.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mutagenesis results.

claim: No density indicating the presence of an NAD+ molecule at the TIR domain active site was found in the NAD+ supplemented structure.
source: Interestingly, we did not find a density indicating the presence of an NAD+ molecule at the TIR domain active site, although this site is not occluded by the ARM domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the NAD+ supplemented cryo-EM map.

claim: The BB loop, which is interacting with a neighboring ARM domain, possibly assumes a conformation that prevents NAD+ entry into the TIR binding cleft.
source: Possibly, the BB loop, which is interacting with a neighboring ARM domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), assumes a conformation that prevents NAD+ entry into the binding cleft.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural analysis.

claim: The difference between the highest and lowest resolution domains (SAM > ARM > TIR) is more obvious in the GraFix-ed structure than the NAD+ supplemented structure.
source: Another conspicuous distinction between the two maps is the difference in local resolution of the domains. The difference between the highest and lowest resolution domains (SAM > ARM > TIR) is more obvious in the GraFix-ed structure than the NAD+ supplemented structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on local resolution analysis of the cryo-EM maps.

claim: There is more flexibility in the GraFix-ed structure compared to the NAD+ supplemented structure.
source: This implies that there is more flexibility in the GraFix-ed structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the difference in local resolution.

claim: The compact arrangement in the GraFix-ed structure is artificially imposed by high glycerol concentration.
source: A likely reason for the difference in map homogeneity is that while the compact arrangement in the GraFix-ed structure is artificially imposed by high glycerol concentration
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental protocol and structural analysis.

claim: The NAD+ supplement seems to induce a more natural compact folding of hSARM1.
source: the NAD+ supplement seems to induce a more natural compact folding.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the difference in map homogeneity.

claim: The octamer ring structure of near-intact hSARM1 reveals an inhibited conformation in which the catalytic TIR domains are kept apart from each other.
source: Our octamer ring structure of a near-intact hSARM1 reveals an inhibited conformation, in which the catalytic TIR domains are kept apart from each other, unable to form close homodimers, which are required for their NADase activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the structural findings.

claim: The inhibited conformation of hSARM1 readily disassembles and gains most of its potential activity during protein purification.
source: This inhibited conformation readily disassembles and gains most of its potential activity during protein purification
evidence: This is based on the observation that purified hSARM1 is mostly active in vitro.

claim: A low-affinity cellular factor that inhibits hSARM1 is lost during purification.
source: substantiating our hypothesis that a low-affinity cellular factor inhibits hSARM1 is lost in purification.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the difference in activity between cellular and in vitro conditions.

claim: NAD+ induces a dramatic conformational shift in purified hSARM1, from a disassembled outer ring to a compact two-ring structure.
source: We have tested a few candidate molecules and found that NAD+ induces a dramatic conformational shift in purified hSARM1, from a disassembled outer ring to a compact two-ring structure, through binding to a distal allosteric site from the TIR catalytic domain.
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data with NAD+ supplement.

claim: Point mutations in the distal allosteric site promoted hSARM1 activity in cultured cells.
source: Point mutations in this distal site promoted hSARM1 activity in cultured cells and demonstrates their key allosteric role for inhibition of the NADase activity.
evidence: This is based on cell viability assays with mutants.

claim: hSARM1 is inhibited in vitro by NAD+ for NADase activity, demonstrating a 'substrate inhibition mechanism'.
source: We also found that hSARM1 is inhibited in vitro by NAD+ for NADase activity, demonstrating a 'substrate inhibition mechanism', as was also reported by another recent study (Jiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on in vitro NADase activity assays and supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2020.

claim: hSARM1 is kept inhibited by NAD+ through its allosteric site located at the ARM domain 'horns' junction.
source: In this model, we suggest that hSARM1 is kept inhibited by NAD+ through its allosteric site, located at the ARM domain 'horns' junction that induces the compact inhibited conformation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: The inhibited state of hSARM1 persists as long as NAD+ remains at normal cellular levels.
source: This state persists as long as NAD+ remains at normal cellular levels (these are controversial and range between 0.1 mM [Cambronne et al., 2016] and 0.4–0.8 mM [Hara et al., 2019; Houtkooper et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2018b]).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model, with citations to studies on cellular NAD+ levels.

claim: Upon a drop in cellular NAD+ concentration below a critical threshold, NAD+ dissociates from the allosteric inhibitory site.
source: However, upon a drop in the cellular NAD+ concentration below a critical threshold, such as in response to stress, NAD+ dissociates from the allosteric inhibitory site.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: Dissociation of NAD+ from the allosteric site triggers the disassembly of the compact conformation and the dimerization of TIR domains.
source: This triggers the disassembly of the compact conformation and the dimerization of TIR domains, which enables TIR's NADase activity and NAD+ hydrolysis.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: The consequence of TIR dimerization and NADase activity is a rapid decrease in NAD+ cellular levels, leading to energetic catastrophe and cell death.
source: The consequence is a rapid decrease in NAD+ cellular levels, leading to energetic catastrophe and cell death.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: NMN will likely form interactions with most of the ARM1 residues as NAD+.
source: It is likely that NMN, a moiety of NAD+, will form interactions with most of the ARM1 residues as NAD+.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural similarity between NMN and NAD+.

claim: NMN will compete with NAD+ and prevent the formation of ARM1–ARM2 NAD+ bridge, resulting in SARM1 NADase activation.
source: By that, NMN will compete with NAD+ and prevent the formation of ARM1–ARM2 NAD+ bridge, the latter stabilizing the inactive conformation of SARM1. Such NAD+ displacement would result with SARM1 NADase activation.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of NMN activation.

claim: High NMN concentrations are required to effectively compete-off the ARM1–ARM2 bound NAD+.
source: Clearly, this will require high NMN concentrations to effectively compete-off the ARM1–ARM2 bound NAD+.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: Only 1 mM NMN (but not 0.2 mM) induces a moderate increase in SARM1 NADase activity at 50 µM NAD+.
source: Indeed, we show (Figure 3E) that only 1 mM NMN (but not 0.2 mM) induces a moderate increase in SARM1 NADase activity at 50 µM NAD+.
evidence: This is based on in vitro NADase activity assays with NMN.

claim: NMN concentrations are not higher than 5 µM, and in any case 10–200 times lower than that of NAD+.
source: as it consistently appears that NMN concentrations are not higher than 5 µM, and in any case 10–200 times lower than that of NAD+ (Di Stefano et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2018b; Sasaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on cellular NMN and NAD+ levels.

claim: While NMN could activate SARM1 in vitro in cultured cells engineered to over produce NMN, or by exogenous supplement of NMN or NMN analogs, it is less likely to occur in vivo.
source: Therefore, while NMN could activate SARM1 in vitro in cultured cells engineered to over produce NMN, or by exogenous supplement of NMN or NMN analogs, it is less likely to occur in vivo
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of NMN and NAD+ concentrations.

claim: The release of substrate inhibition due to the drop in NAD+ levels is the key event in SARM1 activation.
source: suggesting that the release of substrate inhibition due to the drop in NAD+ levels is the key event in SARM1 activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Bratkowski et al., 2020 reported a 3.3 Å cryo-EM structure of hSARM150-724.
source: Very recently, Bratkowski et al., 2020 have reported a 3.3 Å cryo-EM structure of hSARM150-724.
evidence: This is a citation to a recent study.

claim: The structure reported by Bratkowski et al., 2020 is largely similar to the 2.88 Å GraFix-ed structure, except for a residue registry shift throughout the ARM1 α1–α4 and a minor one at the ARM1–ARM2 loop.
source: Except for a residue registry shift throughout the ARM1 α1–α4 and a minor one at the ARM1–ARM2 loop, their structure is largely similar to our 2.88 Å GraFix-ed structure.
evidence: This is a comparison with the structure reported by Bratkowski et al., 2020.

claim: Bratkowski et al. employed a strategy of selectively using a small subset (5.6%) of the initial picked particles to reconstruct their map.
source: It seems that Bratkowski et al. employed a different strategy by selectively using a small subset (5.6%) of the initial picked particles to reconstruct their map.
evidence: This is an inference based on the methods described in Bratkowski et al., 2020.

claim: Bratkowski et al. used selective particle picking to cope with the particle heterogeneity of purified SARM1.
source: We assume that this was done to cope with the particle heterogeneity of purified SARM1. An obstacle we have encountered as well, where we observed that ~80% of the particles have a disordered outer ring.
evidence: This is an inference based on the methods described in Bratkowski et al., 2020 and the authors' own observations.
